Grain addition settings switch to kilograms and grams when the volume setting is either liters or hectoliters.

Calcium content can vary depending on the water source.
Calcium content is sometimes reported (as CaCO

If they don't closely agree, there may be an error in the input units. Use the calculators below to try converting the calcium concentration to the proper ppm units.

Sodium content in drinking water is highly variable. Low to moderate sodium is an important factor in producing good beer. This is a component that should not be ignored.
Sulfate is an important flavor component in brewing water. If the water report result is presented in (SO

-S) (sulfate as sulfur) units, that value must be multiplied by 3 for use in this program.

Some laboratories cater to agricultural clients and those clients are more interested in the total Sulfur content. They report in terms of "Sulfate as Sulphur" which is denoted "SO
-S". The Brewer needs to convert that result to its true sulfate concentration by multiplying the SO
-S result by 3.

The effectiveness of Boiling to reduce Temporary Hardness can vary.
In most cases, the ending bicarbonate concentration will end up between
50 and 80 ppm. Better preboiling technique should end up with lower
bicarbonate content.
To aid in determining what the post-boil water alkalinity is, an Alkalinity Test
kit result for the post-boiled water can be used guide this setting.
Compare the alkalinity test kit result with the Alkalinity value reported
below. Adjust the Boiling Effectiveness setting to approximate your test
result. The Effectiveness setting does not need to be identical to your
test result. Just get the setting close to the alkalinity testing result.

The quantity of cations and anions in water is always equal. However, reporting errors or the presence of ions in the water that were not tested for, will through off that equality. So, perfect agreement is not a requirement. However, the sums should be similar.
This reports the total Cation content calculated from the water report.

This result should be close to zero, but the result does not have to be exactly zero. A difference of 0.1 or less shows good agreement for the cation and anion totals. If the cation and anion totals don't fall within 0.5 meq/L of each other, begin to question the reported concentrations.
Examine each entry and make sure that they are reported in the proper units and convert any that are not in the proper units.
This reports the total Anion content calculated from the water report.
Total Dissolved Solids

indicates the amount of mineralization of the water. It is calculated as the sum of the Cation and Anion concentrations.
Although not very useful to brewing, it can be used as a quick field check between the water report and the tap water. A TDS meter provides a field check of the tap water. The typical meter is accurate to within +/- 4% of the actual TDS value.
Since the tap water may have other ionic content that was not tested for or reported in the lab testing, the TDS meter is more likely to report a higher value than calculated here.
A TDS meter reading is useful for checking water supply variability. When the meter reading differs significantly from this calculated value, the tap water quality may have changed from the reported values.
Total Hardness = ((Ca/20)+(Mg/12.15))*50
Alkalinity is calculated from the bicarbonate and carbonate concentrations.
Permanent Hardness = Total Hardness - Alkalinity

Residual Alkalinity (RA) is an approximate measure of the water's performance during mashing. RA around zero or less may be more suited to pale beer brewing while RA of greater than about 50 may be more suitable for darker beer brewing. RA can be a negative value.
Temporary Hardness = Alkalinity
Total Alkalinity and Temporary Hardness
are typically equal to each other and can
be used to estimate bicarbonate content.
